newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Imperial's debut lights up sector.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Imperial's debut lights up sector.

text.p: Imperial Tobacco Plc, the first of Lord Hanson's "grandchildren" to leave the conglomerate family, marked its demerger from Hanson Plc with a strong London debut on Tuesday which lit up the rest of the tobacco sector.
Imperial, the first company to be spun off in Hanson's four-way split, exceeded expectations with a debut at 390 pence per share, valuing the group at just over 2.0 billion pounds ($3.13 billion).
But analysts warned that selling pressure could come in once Wall Street opened at 1330 GMT, with 30 percent of the stock in U.S. hands.
Imperial chief executive, Gareth Davis, a veteran smoker himself, said he was pleased with the company's performance. "So far, so good," he said.
Speaking from the trading floor at ABN AMRO Hoare Govett, the company's brokers, Davis said: "It seems to have gone well so far. We look forward to the rest of the day."
"It will be interesting when the Americans come in," he added.
The shares had been tipped to trade at between 370 and 380 pence, after sentiment was dampened by news last Friday of a British group court action against Imperial by lung cancer sufferers
Tuesday's London trading showed little sign of litigation jitters. The shares stood at about 393 by the end of the morning session, with volume standing at more than 15 million shares.
B.A.T Industries Plc, Imperial's rival and the biggest British-based tobacco company, also rose on the news. Its shares were up six pence at 430-1/2 pence, with volumes of almost 30 million.
"Imperial has had such a strong opening and that's what's boosted B.A.T," one market maker explained.
Analysts warned that Imperial could have a rockier ride once the U.S. market kicked in.
"U.S. investors hold around 30 percent of Imperial -- which is only listed in the UK. So there may be some selling pressure later on," said Zafar Khan, analyst at Societe Generale Strauss Turnbull.

Explaining why Imperial was performing well in London despite the spectre of court action, Khan said unlike U.S. companies, Imperial did not have damaging internal documents circulating in the public domain and undermining its defence.
"Also, it won't be trial by jury, but by judge," which should stand in Imperial's favour, he added.

Imperial enters the market as one of the most efficient players in the industry. In the 10 years since its was taken over by Hanson Plc it has slashed costs, cut its number of brands to 33 from 150 and raised productivity by 195 percent.
Britain remains Imperial's dominant market. Its trading weakspot is its low penetration of fast growing new markets in India, China and the Far East, where U.S. competitors already have a stronghold.
But Davis has pledged export-led growth in future.
Next on Hanson's demerger list is Millennium Chemicals which starts trading on the New York Stock Exchange on Wednesday.
The Energy Group will be spun off next year, leaving the rump building company which will retain the Hanson family name. ($1=.6387 Pound)
